name: Sidelock of youth

lead: The sidelock of youth was a hairstyle of ancient Egyptian children: the head was shaved and a single braid was left on one side, usually the right. It marked childhood and, for royal children, heirship.
For looks, it is a historical reference people can borrow for a distinctive one-lock style on a shaved head. Its meaning in ancient Egypt was tied to youth and to the child god Horus.

paras: The traditional form was a braid of three strands with the end twisted into a spiral and fixed with a clasp. In art it often appears on a shaved head or attached to a wig.
No known risks beyond those of tight braiding. Not a research topic.

chain: Shaved or cropped head with one side braid
angle.text: The style is a visual look based on one retained lock, used historically as a childhood marker and now borrowed as a distinctive hairstyle.

lead: The sidelock of youth was an identifying hairstyle of children in ancient Egypt, usually a braid of hair from one side of the head, split in three strands and ending in a twisted spiral held by a clasp, generally worn on the right.[1] Egyptologists coined the name; it is also called the Horus lock or prince's lock.[1]

It marked mortal and divine children, and for royal children it signaled heirship; the lock linked them to the youthful god Horus.[1][2] Royal children are shown naked, finger to mouth, with shaved heads except for the lock; later it was often attached to a shoulder-length wig.[1] It appears from the Old Kingdom, was revived in later periods, and was central to depictions of 18th Dynasty princes and princesses.[1]

paras: A three-strand braid on one side of a shaved head, often with the end rolled forward in Middle Kingdom depictions.[1]

Attested from the Old Kingdom, with the Middle Kingdom form revived by Amenhotep I and Thutmose III and again in the Late Period.[1] Examples include Ramesses II as crown prince.[1] Grokipedia describes the style as universal across social classes and cut at the transition to adulthood; that account is AI-generated.[2]

timeline.event: Earliest attested use as a divine attribute.[1]
Central symbol of princes and princesses of the 18th Dynasty.[1]
